title: Matching pairs
keyIdea: A pair is two things that are the same. To match, look at everything: the colour, the shape, the size and the pattern. A red spotty sock and a red stripy sock are both red, but they are not a pair. Say 'same' when two things match, and say how: 'same colour, same spots'.

kid: A pair is two things that are the same. Two socks. Two shoes. Two gloves.
Look at the colour. Look at the shape. Look at the size. Look for spots or stripes.
Two red socks are not a pair if one has spots and one has stripes. A big duck and a little duck are not a pair.
When you find two the same, say 'Same!' Then say how: 'Same colour. Same spots.'
adult: Matching is one of the first maths skills. In the EYFS framework it sits in Mathematics (birth to three and three and four year olds in Development Matters): noticing what is the same and what is different, comparing sizes, and spotting patterns. Matching pairs leads straight into sorting by an attribute (colour, shape, size), into one-to-one correspondence (one cup for each teddy), and later into counting, where each object is touched once.

Young children often match on one feature only. They see red and stop looking, so a red stripy sock 'goes with' a red spotty sock. The fix is to name every attribute out loud: 'Both red. Spots or stripes?' Size is the other common slip: a big duck and a little duck are both ducks, but they are not the same.

The language matters as much as the matching. Use 'same', 'not the same', 'pair', 'match' and 'different', and ask 'How do you know they match?' A child who can say 'same colour, same spots' is starting to reason about attributes, not just guessing.

In the lab your child hangs each sock beside its pair (with a red stripy decoy), plays a turn-over-two-cards pairs game, says same or not the same, finds the lonely item with no pair, and puts each lid on the pot that matches its size.

familyTip: Sort the clean socks together. Hold one up and ask: 'Can you find the one that is the same?' Then ask: 'How do you know?' Leave out one odd sock and ask which one has no pair.

practice.prompt: Which sock goes with a blue stripy sock?
practice.hint: Look at the colour and the pattern. Both must be the same.
practice.explain: A blue stripy sock. Same colour and same stripes, so they are a pair.

practice.prompt: There are {n} socks. They are all the same. Are they all one colour?
practice.hint: Things that are the same have the same colour.
practice.explain: Yes. The {n} socks are all the same, so they are all one colour.

practice.prompt: A big teddy and a little teddy. Are they a pair?
choices: No, one is big and one is little
practice.hint: A pair is the same size too.
practice.explain: No. They are both teddies, but one is big and one is little. Not the same size.

practice.prompt: You have {n} shoes. They make pairs. How many shoes are in one pair?
practice.hint: A pair is two things that are the same.
practice.explain: 2. A pair is always two. Your {n} shoes make pairs of two.

choices: Two things that are the same
pool.hint: Think of two socks that match.
pool.explain: A pair is two things that are the same, like two socks or two gloves.

pool.prompt: A red circle and a red square. Are they the same?
pool.hint: Look at the shape, not just the colour.
pool.explain: No. Both are red, but one is round and one is a square.

pool.prompt: Which one has no pair: apple, pear, apple, pear, orange?
pool.hint: Find the two apples and the two pears first.
pool.explain: The orange. There are two apples and two pears, but only one orange.

pool.prompt: Which lid fits the little pot?
pool.hint: The lid must be the same size as the pot.
pool.explain: The little lid. It is the same size, so it fits. A big lid wobbles off.

pool.prompt: You turn over {n} cards. Two show a dog. Do the two dogs match?
pool.hint: Look at the two pictures. Are they the same?
pool.explain: Yes. Two dogs that look the same are a pair, even if you turned over {n} cards.

pool.prompt: There are {n} pairs of socks. One sock is lost. How many socks have no pair?
pool.hint: One sock is lost. What about its partner?
pool.explain: 1. When one sock is lost, its partner is left on its own, with no pair. The other {=n-1} pairs are fine.

pool.prompt: Two green gloves match. How do you know?
choices: They are both on the floor
pool.hint: Say what is the same about them.
pool.explain: Same colour and same shape. Saying how they match shows you looked closely.
